questions.problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x=\frac{1}{{t}^{3}},\,y=\frac{3}{t}.$ Given that $\frac{dy}{dx}={t}^{2},$ calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\frac{dy}{dx}={t}^{2},$ and we can calculate $\frac{dx}{dt}$ as follows:

$$
\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{1}{{t}^{3}})=-\frac{3}{{t}^{4}}
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}({t}^{2})}{(-\frac{3}{{t}^{4}})} \\  & =\frac{2t}{(-\frac{3}{{t}^{4}})} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}{t}^{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t),\,y=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)-2.$ Given that $\frac{dy}{dx}=2\operatorname{tan}⁡(3t),$ calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\frac{dy}{dx}=2\operatorname{tan}⁡(3t),$ and we can calculate $\frac{dx}{dt}$ as follows:

$$
\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t))=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(2\operatorname{tan}⁡(3t))}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)} \\  & =\frac{6{sec}^{2}⁡(3t)}{3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)} \\  & =2{sec}^{3}⁡(3t).\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\frac{dy}{dx}=3{e}^{2t}-1,$ and we can calculate $\frac{dx}{dt}$ as follows:

$$

$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(3{e}^{2t}-1)}{{e}^{t}} \\  & =\frac{6{e}^{2t}}{{e}^{t}} \\  & =6{e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-10,\,y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+15.$ Calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the first derivative, we will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t),\,{y}^{′}(t)=24\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t).
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{24\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)}{8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)}=3\operatorname{cot}⁡(4t).
$$

To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(3\operatorname{cot}⁡(4t))}{8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)} \\  & =-\frac{12{csc}^{2}⁡(4t)}{8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}{csc}^{3}⁡(4t).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x=\frac{{t}^{3}}{3},\,y={t}^{5}+2{t}^{3}$ where $t$ is a real number. Calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the first derivative, we will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)={t}^{2},\,{y}^{′}(t)=5{t}^{4}+6{t}^{2}.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{5{t}^{4}+6{t}^{2}}{{t}^{2}}=5{t}^{2}+6.
$$

To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(5{t}^{2}+6)}{{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{10t}{{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{10}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x =e^{t}, \, y= e^{2t}+1.$ Given that $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}= 2e^t,$ calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d^2 y}{\textrm d x^2}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}= 2e^t,$ and we can calculate $\dfrac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}$ as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt} = \dfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt} (e^t) = e^t
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(2{e}^{t})}{{e}^{t}} \\  & =\frac{2{e}^{t}}{{e}^{t}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x=e^t, y=2e^{2t}.$ Calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d^2 y}{\textrm d x^2}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the first derivative, we will use the formula

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
x'(t) = e^t, \qquad y'(t)=4e^{2t}.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x} = \dfrac{4e^{2t}}{e^t} = 4e^t.
$$

To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(4{e}^{t})}{{e}^{t}} \\  & =\frac{4{e}^{t}}{{e}^{t}} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Calculating the Derivative of a Parametric Curve at a Given Point
canonical_examples.problem:
A curve is defined by the parametric equations 

$$
x =  \sin(2t), \qquad y= 2\cos (2t) \qquad 0 \leq t \lt \pi.
$$

Given that $\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} = -2 \tan(2t),$ calculate $\dfrac{\textrm d^2 y}{\textrm d x^2}$ at the point where $t=\dfrac\pi 8.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To compute $\dfrac{\textrm d^2 y }{\textrm d x^2},$ we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}= -2 \tan(2t),$ and we can calculate $\dfrac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt}$ as follows:

$$
\dfrac{\mathrm dx}{\mathrm dt} = \dfrac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt} ( \sin 2t ) = 2 \cos(2t).
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(-2\operatorname{tan}⁡2t)}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)} \\  & =\frac{-4{sec}^{2}⁡(2t)}{2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)} \\  & =-4{sec}^{2}⁡(2t)\cdot \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sec}⁡(2t) \\  & =-2{sec}^{3}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{8},$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}{|}_{t=\pi /8} & =-2{sec}^{3}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{8}) \\  & =-2{sec}^{3}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =-2{(\sqrt{2})}^{3} \\  & =-4\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$
